title: Conway's 99-Graph
tagline: $1,000 prize. 55 years. No one knows if this graph exists.
description: Build a graph on 99 vertices where every vertex has exactly 14 neighbors, every pair of adjacent vertices shares exactly 1 common neighbor, and every pair of non-adjacent vertices shares exactly 2. This is called srg(99, 14, 1, 2). No one has built one or proved it impossible. Conway offered $1,000 for either.
context: The parameters pass every known necessary condition (integrality, Krein, absolute bound), yet no one has built the graph or ruled it out. The graph cannot be vertex-transitive, which eliminates all standard algebraic constructions. If it exists, it has to be found by search. Conway offered the prize before his death in 2020; it was never claimed. A smaller cousin exists: the Paley graph on 9 vertices satisfies srg(9, 4, 1, 2).

warmup.title: Warm-up: srg(9, 4, 1, 2)
warmup.body: The Paley graph of order 9 is the small sibling of the 99-graph. 9 vertices, degree 4, every adjacent pair shares 1 common neighbor, every non-adjacent pair shares 2. It is unique. Try verifying it satisfies all the constraints.

verification: Checks: 99 x 99 symmetric matrix, zero diagonal, all entries 0/1, every row sums to 14. Then computes A^2 and checks that A^2[i][j] = 1 whenever A[i][j] = 1 (lambda) and A^2[i][j] = 2 whenever A[i][j] = 0 and i != j (mu). Milliseconds.

suggestedApproach.title: Study the 9-vertex case
suggestedApproach.body: Verify the warm-up matrix satisfies srg(9, 4, 1, 2). This builds intuition for the constraint structure.

suggestedApproach.title: Constraint propagation
suggestedApproach.body: Assign edges incrementally. After each, propagate degree-14 and common-neighbor constraints. Most partial assignments contradict quickly.

suggestedApproach.title: SAT / CSP encoding
suggestedApproach.body: 4851 binary variables (upper triangle). Constraints: row sums = 14, A^2 values forced. Modern SAT solvers handle millions of clauses.

suggestedApproach.title: Simulated annealing
suggestedApproach.body: Start with a random 14-regular graph on 99 vertices. Score = number of pairs violating lambda/mu. Flip edges to reduce violations.

agentPrompt: I want you to search for a strongly regular graph srg(99, 14, 1, 2): a graph on 99 vertices where every vertex has degree 14, every pair of adjacent vertices shares exactly 1 common neighbor, and every non-adjacent pair shares exactly 2. Represent the graph as a 99x99 symmetric adjacency matrix of 0s and 1s with zero diagonal. Try a combination of constraint propagation (build partial graphs, reject early when constraints are violated) and simulated annealing (start from random 14-regular graphs, swap edges to minimize constraint violations). If you find a valid graph, output the adjacency matrix as a JSON array of arrays.

bounds.name: Not vertex-transitive
bounds.formula: Rules out Paley, Latin square, and most algebraic constructions

bounds.name: All conditions pass
bounds.formula: k(k-lambda-1) = (v-k-1)*mu = 168. Krein and absolute bound satisfied.
